## 2. The extracted sprite atlas

Everything below is now in `assets\ui\ui-atlas.json`, generated by `tools\extract-ui-spec.ps1`. Nothing here was typed in by hand: every size is a `System.Drawing` measurement, every nine-slice border is read from the sprite's own `.mcmeta` sidecar, and every drawn rectangle is the measured bounding box of non-transparent pixels. **The art owns the numbers and the script reads them**, which is the only arrangement this project has found that does not rot.

### 2.1 What was catalogued

**576 sprites in 57 groups**, from two sources:

| Source | Sprites | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `reference\minecraft-assets-26.2\...\textures\gui\` | 555 | The modern Java 1.21 GUI tree, already split into individual sprites |
| `reference\ui-icons\` | 21 | The Bedrock crafting-screen crops this project cut itself, 1x measured, 3x recorded alongside |

Every group carries a `relevance` field, which is the one judgement call in the file and is **recorded rather than acted on** - nothing is filtered out on the strength of it:

| Relevance | Groups | Sprites | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core` | 23 | 309 | A screen this game has or wants |
| `reference` | 25 | 190 | Worth reading, not on the route |
| `unused` | 9 | 77 | Realms and multiplayer, which is permanently cut |

### 2.2 The `.mcmeta` find

Modern Minecraft ships a JSON sidecar beside a GUI sprite declaring how it scales. **There are exactly 50 of them in the gui tree, and they are the authoritative nine-slice border data** - the thing that turns a 200x20 button PNG into a button of any size at all. They split:

- **44 declare `gui.scaling`, all of them `nine_slice`.** Not one sprite in this drop declares `tile`; the mode is documented in the atlas header anyway, so meeting the third one later is not a surprise.
- **6 declare `animation` instead** - a vertical strip of frames, not one picture. Recorded with the real frame size, because `hud/locator_bar_arrow_up` is a 7x10 file that draws as 7x5.
- **The other 532 sprites have no sidecar at all.** Their scaling is `stretch` by default, and the atlas writes `"scaling":"stretch"` on every one of them explicitly. A reader never has to know the default, and a missing sidecar can never be confused with an unfinished entry.

Two things the border can be, both normalised to four sides in the output so a reader only ever meets one form: a single number for all four sides (`"border":10`), or an object naming each (`"border":{"left":17,"top":30,"right":4,"bottom":4}`).

**All 44 declared sizes agreed with the measured PNG**, checked rather than assumed - the atlas has a `declared` field that appears only on a disagreement, and it appears nowhere. So the borders are known to have been measured against the art that shipped.

### 2.3 The schema

One header block, then groups, then one sprite per line - deliberately, so `findstr "widget/button"` answers a question without a JSON parser and a diff shows exactly which sprites moved.

```json
{
  "schema": "ui-atlas", "schemaVersion": 1, "generated": "2026-08-17",
  "generator": "tools/extract-ui-spec.ps1",
  "note": "GENERATED FILE - do not hand-edit...",
  "reference": "minecraft-assets-26.2", "referenceRoot": "reference",
  "spriteCount": 576, "groupCount": 57,
  "nineSliceCount": 44, "stretchCount": 532, "animatedCount": 6,
  "scalingModes": { "stretch": "...", "nine_slice": "...", "tile": "..." },
  "fields": { "opaque": "...", "declared": "...", "animation": "...", "relevance": "..." },
  "groups": [
    {
      "id": "widget", "title": "Shared widgets",
      "source": "minecraft-assets-26.2/.../textures/gui/sprites/widget",
      "relevance": "core", "count": 33, "nineSliceCount": 16,
      "purpose": "The controls every screen is built from...",
      "sprites": [
        {"id":"widget/button","path":".../sprites/widget/button.png","width":200,"height":20,
         "scaling":"nine_slice","border":{"left":3,"top":3,"right":3,"bottom":3},
         "center":{"width":194,"height":14},"mcmeta":".../button.png.mcmeta",
         "purpose":"The standard button. Nine-sliced with a 3px border..."}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Per-sprite fields, in order: `id`, `path`, `width`, `height`, `scaling`, then `border` and `center` (nine-slice only), `stretchInner`, `declared`, `animation`, `opaque`, `fullyTransparent`, `mcmeta`, `purpose`. **Everything after `scaling` appears only when it has something to say**, so the absence of a field is itself information rather than an omission.

Two fields are derived rather than copied, and that is the point:

- **`center`** is `width - left - right` by `height - top - bottom`. It is the part that actually stretches. Deriving it once here means nobody subtracts it by hand at a call site and gets it wrong the one time it is asymmetric.
- **`opaque`** is the measured bounding box of every non-transparent pixel, written only when the art does not fill the file. **This is how the classic 176x166 inventory rectangle inside a 256x256 page is known** - read off the art, not remembered. 274 of the 576 sprites have one.

### 2.5 The important twenty

The sprites most likely to be reused, with their borders spelled out. `L T R B` are the nine-slice insets; `centre` is what stretches.

| Sprite | Size | Scaling | L T R B | Centre | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `widget/button` | 200x20 | nine_slice | 3 3 3 3 | 194x14 | Every button in the game, at any size, from one file |
| `widget/button_highlighted` | 200x20 | nine_slice | 3 3 3 3 | 194x14 | Hover state, identical geometry |
| `widget/button_disabled` | 200x20 | nine_slice | 1 1 1 1 | 198x18 | Border drops to 1 - the disabled art has no inner bevel to preserve |
| `widget/tab` | 130x24 | nine_slice | 2 2 2 **0** | 126x22 | The instructive one: a **bottom border of 0** is what makes a tab join the panel below instead of closing against it |
| `widget/tab_selected` | 130x24 | nine_slice | 2 2 2 **0** | 126x22 | Same open bottom edge |
| `widget/text_field` | 200x20 | nine_slice | 1 1 1 1 | 198x18 | Any text input |
| `widget/slider` | 200x20 | nine_slice | 1 1 1 1 | 198x18 | The trough |
| `widget/slider_handle` | 8x20 | nine_slice | 2 2 2 **3** | 4x15 | **Asymmetric**: 3 at the bottom because the knob has a taller shadow under it than highlight above |
| `widget/scroller` | 6x32 | nine_slice | 1 1 1 1 | 4x30 | The thumb, shortens as a list grows |
| `widget/scroller_background` | 6x32 | nine_slice | 1 1 1 1 | 4x30 | The trough behind it |
| `tooltip/background` | 100x100 | nine_slice | 9 9 9 9 | 82x82 | The flat fill behind tooltip text |
| `tooltip/frame` | 100x100 | nine_slice | 10 10 10 10 | 80x80 | The gradient border over it, and **the only sprite in the whole set with `stretch_inner`** - its middle stretches rather than tiles, which is what keeps a tall tooltip's gradient clean |
| `container/slot` | 18x18 | stretch | - | - | **The number the whole game is laid out against.** No margin of its own, so slots tile at an 18px pitch and a 9x3 grid is exactly 162x54 |
| `container/slot_highlight_front` | 24x24 | nine_slice | 4 4 4 4 | 16x16 | Hover wash over the item - 24 against an 18 well means it overhangs by 3 on every side |
| `container/slot_highlight_back` | 24x24 | nine_slice | 4 4 4 4 | 16x16 | The same wash under the item |
| `container/inventory/effect_background` | 32x32 | nine_slice | 4 4 4 4 | 24x24 | Status-effect panel beside the inventory, stretches to the longest name |
| `recipe_book/overlay_recipe` | 32x32 | nine_slice | 4 4 4 4 | 24x24 | The panel that fans out when a recipe is clicked |
| `popup/background` | 236x34 | nine_slice | 6 6 6 6 | 224x22 | A modal box over a screen |
| `toast/system` | 160x64 | nine_slice | **17 30 4 4** | 139x30 | **The most asymmetric nine-slice here** - the icon well and title bar are baked into the top-left corners |
| `toast/tutorial` | 160x32 | nine_slice | 3 3 3 3 | 154x26 | The ordinary toast shape |
| `hud/hotbar` | 182x22 | stretch | - | - | 182 = 1 + 9x20 + 1. Nine slots at a 20px pitch with a 1px frame, and `hud/hotbar_selection` at 24x23 overhangs it on purpose |
| `hud/heart/container` | 9x9 | stretch | - | - | Every one of the 47 hearts is 9x9, no exceptions |
| `boss_bar/purple_background` | 182x5 | stretch | - | - | All 22 boss bars are 182x5 - **the hotbar width**, which is also `hud/experience_bar_background`'s width, and that is what aligns the three |
| `hud/locator_bar_background` | 12x5 | nine_slice | **5 1 5 1** | 2x3 | The only nine-slice whose left/right insets exceed its top/bottom: almost all border, stretching through a 2x3 centre |

Only twelve distinct border shapes exist across all 44: `1,1,1,1`, `2,2,2,2`, `2,2,2,0`, `2,2,2,3`, `3,3,3,3`, `4,4,4,4`, `5,1,5,1`, `6,6,6,6`, `8,8,8,8`, `9,9,9,9`, `10,10,10,10` and `17,30,4,4`. **Eight of the twelve are uniform, four are not** - so a nine-slice draw routine that only took one number would work for most of the set and be silently wrong for a tab, a slider handle, the locator bar and the system toast, which is exactly the shape of bug this project keeps paying for.

### 2.6 The container screen rectangles, measured

The 23 pre-split sheets under `gui\container\` are 256x256 (villager 512x256) pages whose screen occupies the top-left corner only. **Those rectangles were derived from the alpha channel, not remembered**, and they are on every entry as `opaque`:

| Screen | Sheet | Drawn |
|---|---|---|
| `screen/inventory`, `crafting_table`, `furnace`, `anvil`, `enchanting_table`, `dispenser`, `brewing_stand`, `shulker_box`, `horse`, `loom`, `smithing`, `smoker`, `blast_furnace`, `stonecutter`, `grindstone`, `cartography_table`, `crafter`, `nautilus` | 256x256 | **176x166** |
| `screen/generic_54` (double chest) | 256x256 | **176x222** - the tallest |
| `screen/hopper` | 256x256 | **176x133** |
| `screen/beacon` | 256x256 | **230x219** |
| `screen/villager` | 512x256 | **276x166** - the only sheet needing a 512-wide page |
| `screen/gamemode_switcher` | 128x128 | 125x75 |

**Eighteen of twenty-three screens are the same 176x166.** That is the single most reusable geometric fact in the whole extraction: a container screen is 176x166 unless it has a reason not to be, and the four that differ each have one.

### 2.7 Traps the measurement turned up

Things a reader would otherwise discover by wondering why nothing drew:

- **Three sprites are entirely transparent** and are flagged `"fullyTransparent": true`: `background/tab_header_background` (16x16), `container/loom/error` (26x26) and `panorama/panorama_overlay` (**1x1**). The panorama overlay in particular is a single transparent pixel - the title screen's darkening is no longer art, so copying "there is an overlay texture" would mean chasing a file with nothing in it.
- **Six sprites are frame strips, not pictures.** `hud/locator_bar_arrow_up` and `_down` are 7x10 files of two 7x5 frames; `icon/music_notes` is 16x128 of eight 16x16; `icon/trial_available` is 8x48 of six 8x8; `realm_status/expires_soon` is 10x56 of two 10x28; `friends/loading` is 5x6 of three 5x2. Reading the file height as the sprite height is wrong for every one of them, and the atlas carries `animation.frameHeight` so nobody has to.
- **The three cooking screens share their geometry exactly.** Furnace, smoker and blast furnace all use a 24x16 progress arrow and a 14x14 flame; only the art differs. One drawing routine serves all three - and an early draft of this fragment claimed they were sized differently, which the measurement caught.
- **`bedrock/toggle-craftable` is a 28x19 crop of a 26x16 control.** The crop was cut with a margin. `recipe_book/filter_enabled` measures 26x16 exactly, so the Java sprite is the one to size against and the Bedrock crop is the one to look at. Every Bedrock entry carries the same warning in its group purpose: the source was a lossy AVIF console capture at 3x, so those sizes are a recovered grid, not a clean rip.
- **`bedrock/slot-empty` measures 18x18**, the same as Java's `container/slot`. The two editions' slot pitch is identical, which is what makes the layouts directly comparable.

### 2.8 Regenerating it

```
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\extract-ui-spec.ps1          # write
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\extract-ui-spec.ps1 -Check   # fail if stale
```

Both were run. The first writes `assets\ui\ui-atlas.json` (201,798 bytes, UTF-8 with no BOM, pure ASCII, valid JSON - parsed before it is written); the second reports `up to date` and exits 0. Staleness and a missing file were both tested deliberately and both exit 1 with a message naming the fix.

Four things about the script worth knowing before editing it:

1. **`-Check` normalises the `generated` date on both sides before comparing.** Without that the file would be called stale every morning and rewritten for nothing. For the same reason a run that changes no content leaves the file, and its date, alone.
2. **An undescribed folder throws.** Every folder in the gui tree that holds PNGs must appear in the `$groups` table; one that does not stops the run rather than being silently skipped. A newer reference drop cannot quietly lose sprites. This guard fired on the first run - `gui\sprites` itself holds no PNGs and is structure, not a group - and was narrowed to folders that actually contain art.
3. **A missing `reference\` is reported by name**, with the tool that refills it, because that folder is gitignored and genuinely absent on a fresh clone.
4. **Purposes are curated where a sprite deserves a sentence and templated from the group where it does not.** Adding a line to the `$curated` table is the way to improve the atlas; writing prose in a document nothing checks is not.

**No pixels were copied.** `reference\` is gitignored and never ships; `assets\ui\ui-atlas.json` is metadata about it and nothing more.

## 3. The UI palette, measured

Every colour below came out of `Bitmap.GetPixel` on a file in this repository. Nothing is quoted from memory, nothing is eyeballed off a screenshot, and nothing is averaged between the two design languages. **221 entries** are recorded in `assets\ui\ui-palette.json`: **204 measured** from pixels, **17 documented** (the sixteen `§` formatting codes and the text-shadow rule, sourced from minecraft.wiki and cross-checked against measured art), and **6 flagged `lossy_source`** because the only image carrying them is AVIF- or JPEG-compressed.

They were re-verified after the fact by a script that walks the JSON, opens each cited file, calls `GetPixel` at each recorded `(x, y)` and compares the result to the recorded hex. **201 of 201 re-readable entries matched exactly**; the twenty skipped are the 17 documented values and 3 `rect_mean` averages, which have no single pixel to check. That pass caught five wrong coordinates that had survived the original measurement — proof that "I sampled it" is not the same as "the number and the coordinate agree," and the reason the coordinates in the JSON are worth trusting.

Provenance roots used in every table below:

| Short | Path |
|---|---|
| `J:` | `reference\minecraft-assets-26.2\minecraft-assets-26.2\assets\minecraft\textures\gui\` |
| `S:` | `reference\minecraft-assets-26.2\Minecraft menu and settings screens\` |
| `I:` | `reference\ui-icons\` |
| `R:` | repo root |

Hex is `#RRGGBBAA` throughout. **Alpha is never assumed** — several of the most important values are translucent and would be wrong at `FF`.

---

### 3.1 Two visual languages, and why they must never be averaged

The reference material contains two complete, unrelated design systems. Mixing them produces the exact "not quite right" feeling this exercise exists to prevent.

**The classic Java container language** — used by every in-world screen: inventory, crafting, furnace, chest, anvil, beacon. It is built from a **six-rung grey ladder and nothing else**. The histogram of the 176×166 GUI rect of `J:container/crafting_table.png` contains exactly six opaque colours plus transparent corner notches:

| Rung | Hex | Share of the crafting-table rect | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `#FFFFFFFF` | 6.6% | outer highlight, slot bottom-right |
| 1 | `#C6C6C6FF` | **40.5%** | panel fill |
| 2 | `#8B8B8BFF` | 14.9% | slot fill |
| 3 | `#555555FF` | 5.4% | panel bottom-right shadow |
| 4 | `#373737FF` | 4.1% | slot top-left shadow |
| 5 | `#000000FF` | 3.5% | outer border |

Provenance: `J:container/crafting_table.png`, histogram of rect `(0,0,176,166)`; the individual pixels are cited per row in §3.2. **The same six values, at the same coordinates, appear byte-identically in `inventory.png`, `generic_54.png`, `furnace.png`, `anvil.png`, `beacon.png` and `villager2.png`** — this is one shared chrome, not six similar ones.

Two of those six are not arbitrary: `#AAAAAA` (the button's upper bevel, §3.4) is *exactly* `§7 gray`, and `#555555` is *exactly* `§8 dark_gray`. The chrome and the text palette are drawn from the same well.

**The Bedrock "Ore UI" language** — used by the out-of-world menus: Play, Settings, Create New World, Pause. Flat dark panels, a green accent, one-pixel bevels that are all *lighter* than their fill, and a heavy dark "base lip" doing the 3D work. Its dominant colours are `#48494A` (content pane, 56.7% of the Settings General screen) and `#313233` (navigation rail, 24.3%), with `#3C8527` green as the single accent. There is no grey ladder, no black outline around panels, and **no beige anywhere**.

Our in-world screens follow the first. The out-of-world menus follow the second. `ui-palette.json` groups them under `java_container` / `states` and `bedrock_screen` respectively, and its header carries an explicit `warning` field saying not to blend them.

**`#C6C6C6` held up.** It is the true panel grey by a wide margin — 40.5% of the container rect, present at every panel-fill coordinate tested, and identical across six containers. It is also, independently, Bedrock's `§7 gray`. The widely-quoted number was a hypothesis and it survived measurement.

### 3.2 The classic panel

Sampled by scanning a horizontal run across the left edge at y=4 and a vertical run down the right edge at x=173, so the ramp is read rather than a single pixel guessed.

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.panel.corner_notch` | `#00000000` | `J:container/crafting_table.png` | 0,0 | corners are notched 2–3px transparent, not square |
| `java.panel.border` | `#000000FF` | `J:container/crafting_table.png` | 0,4 | 1px hard black outline, all four sides |
| `java.panel.bevel_light` | `#FFFFFFFF` | `J:container/crafting_table.png` | 1,4 | 2px pure-white highlight, top and left |
| `java.panel.fill` | `#C6C6C6FF` | `J:container/crafting_table.png` | 4,4 | the panel grey |
| `java.panel.bevel_dark` | `#555555FF` | `J:container/crafting_table.png` | 173,80 | 2px shadow, bottom and right |

The run across `y=4` reads, left to right: `000000` ×1, `FFFFFF` ×2, then `C6C6C6` to the far side, then `555555` ×2, then `000000` ×1. **The highlight and shadow are two pixels wide, not one** — this is the single most commonly mis-copied detail of the classic look.

The modern popup frame is a *different* recipe — a light outer frame wrapping a dark interior:

| `java.popup.inner_border` | `#000000FF` | `J:sprites/popup/background.png` | 5,5 | second black line inside the frame |
| `java.popup.fill` | `#303030FF` | `J:sprites/popup/background.png` | 6,6 | dark interior |

### 3.3 Slots and their states

The slot is the panel recipe **run backwards**, and that inversion is the whole trick of the sunken look.

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.slot.shadow` | `#373737FF` | `J:sprites/container/slot.png` | 0,0 | 1px, top and left |
| `java.slot.fill` | `#8B8B8BFF` | `J:sprites/container/slot.png` | 8,8 | empty-slot fill |
| `java.slot.highlight` | `#FFFFFFFF` | `J:sprites/container/slot.png` | 17,17 | 1px, bottom and right |
| `java.slot.corner_offdiagonal` | `#8B8B8BFF` | `J:sprites/container/slot.png` | 17,0 | **the two off-diagonal corners take the fill**, not either bevel |

That last row is the detail everyone gets wrong. At `(17,0)` — top-right — and `(0,17)` — bottom-left — the sprite is `#8B8B8B`, the fill colour. The bevels do not meet at the corners; they stop and the fill runs through. The slot is 18×18 with a 16×16 item area.

**Hover is two separate translucent white layers**, drawn back and front of the item:

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.slot.hover_back` | `#FFFFFF60` | `J:sprites/container/slot_highlight_back.png` | 12,12 | behind the item — white at **alpha 96** |
| `java.slot.hover_front` | `#FFFFFF20` | `J:sprites/container/slot_highlight_front.png` | 12,12 | in front of the item — white at **alpha 32** |

Both sprites are a uniform fill of that value across their whole area; there is no gradient. Guessing "white overlay" and picking any single alpha would have been wrong twice.

**Disabled slot** (the crafter's locked cell) inverts back to the raised look and adds a fourth colour for the corners:

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.slot.disabled.bevel_light` | `#FFFFFFFF` | `J:sprites/container/crafter/disabled_slot.png` | 0,0 | top-left — *light*, the opposite of a normal slot |
| `java.slot.disabled.fill` | `#C6C6C6FF` | `J:sprites/container/crafter/disabled_slot.png` | 8,8 | fill is the panel grey — the cell reads as filled-in |
| `java.slot.disabled.bevel_dark` | `#8B8B8BFF` | `J:sprites/container/crafter/disabled_slot.png` | 17,17 | bottom-right |
| `java.slot.disabled.corner_offdiagonal` | `#B2B2B2FF` | `J:sprites/container/crafter/disabled_slot.png` | 17,0 | a fifth grey, off the ladder, corners only |

**The red states.** `I:slot-red-uncraftable@3x.png` and `I:slot-output-red@3x.png` are AVIF-lossy and their fills smear; the *lossless* red state lives in the Java recipe book, and it is structurally byte-identical to the craftable one with greys swapped for reds of the same value:

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.recipe.craftable.frame` | `#CCCCCCFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_craftable.png` | 0,0 | outer frame |
| `java.recipe.craftable.bevel_dark` | `#373737FF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_craftable.png` | 1,1 | inner top-left |
| `java.recipe.craftable.fill` | `#8B8B8BFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_craftable.png` | 2,2 | cell fill |
| `java.recipe.craftable.bevel_light` | `#FFFFFFFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_craftable.png` | 22,2 | inner bottom-right |
| `java.recipe.craftable.drop` | `#000000FF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_craftable.png` | 24,1 | 1px drop shadow, right and bottom |
| `java.recipe.uncraftable.frame` | `#8A2222FF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_uncraftable.png` | 0,0 | outer frame |
| `java.recipe.uncraftable.bevel_dark` | `#501B1BFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_uncraftable.png` | 1,1 | inner top-left |
| `java.recipe.uncraftable.fill` | `#6A6A6AFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_uncraftable.png` | 2,2 | **fill stays a desaturated grey**, not red |
| `java.recipe.uncraftable.bevel_light` | `#C24F4FFF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_uncraftable.png` | 22,2 | inner bottom-right |
| `java.recipe.uncraftable.drop` | `#000000FF` | `J:sprites/recipe_book/slot_uncraftable.png` | 24,1 | identical drop shadow |

The uncraftable fill being `#6A6A6A` — grey, and *darker* than the craftable `#8B8B8B` — is the part memory gets wrong. Only the frame and the two bevels go red; the cell interior desaturates and dims.

Bedrock's own slot, at 3×, is the same three colours as Java's with one pixel of drift:

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bedrock.slot.empty_shadow` | `#373737FF` | `I:slot-empty@3x.png` | 3,0 | top-left — identical to Java |
| `bedrock.slot.empty_fill` | `#8B8B8BFF` | `I:slot-empty@3x.png` | 47,3 | fill — identical to Java |
| `bedrock.slot.empty_highlight` | `#FEFEFEFF` | `I:slot-empty@3x.png` | 0,3 | bottom-right — `FE`, not `FF` |
| `bedrock.slot.red_highlight` | `#F5786BFF` | `I:slot-red-uncraftable@3x.png` | 1,26 | *lossy source* |
| `bedrock.slot.red_fill` | `#E15547FF` | `R:reference/crafting-ui.png` | 176,292 | *lossy source* |
| `bedrock.slot.red_shadow` | `#5B1C15FF` | `I:slot-red-uncraftable@3x.png` | 52,26 | *lossy source* |

**Use the Java recipe-book reds for anything authored; the Bedrock reds are recorded for completeness and flagged lossy in the JSON.**

### 3.4 Widgets

Java's widgets are **dithered** — the button body is 22 distinct greys — so a single `GetPixel` on the body is not the answer. Fills below are the *histogram mode*: the most frequent colour in the region. `#6F6F6F` is 41.1% of `button.png`'s body.

| `java.button.fill` | `#6F6F6FFF` | `J:sprites/widget/button.png` | 4,3 | body (histogram mode) |
| `java.button.bevel_dark` | `#565656FF` | `J:sprites/widget/button.png` | 198,10 | bottom and right |

| `java.button.hover.bevel_light` | `#AFAFAFFF` | `J:sprites/widget/button_highlighted.png` | 1,10 | +5 per channel |
| `java.button.hover.fill` | `#757575FF` | `J:sprites/widget/button_highlighted.png` | 4,3 | +6 per channel |
| `java.button.hover.bevel_dark` | `#5C5C5CFF` | `J:sprites/widget/button_highlighted.png` | 198,10 | +6 per channel |
| `java.button.disabled.outline` | `#000000FF` | `J:sprites/widget/button_disabled.png` | 0,10 | outline survives |

**Hover is not a new palette, it is the same palette brightened by six.** Body `+6`, lower bevel `+6`, upper bevel `+5`, and the identical dither pattern underneath — both sprites have their mode at 41.1%. The one real change is the outline flipping from black to white. Disabled is the odd one out: it discards the bevel altogether and becomes a flat `#2C2C2C` slab, so a disabled button is not "the button, dimmed" — it is a different shape of thing.

**Tabs are alpha-driven, not colour-driven** — which is why they are impossible to get right by guessing hex:

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.tab.body` | `#000000DB` | `J:sprites/widget/tab.png` | 4,10 | black at **alpha 219** |
| `java.tab.edge` | `#000000BF` | `J:sprites/widget/tab.png` | 0,10 | black at **alpha 191** |

| `java.tab.selected_body` | `#00000000` | `J:sprites/widget/tab_selected.png` | 4,10 | **selected tab is fully transparent** |
| `java.tab.selected_top_edge` | `#000000BF` | `J:sprites/widget/tab_selected.png` | 4,0 | only its top edge survives |

Selection here means *removing* the tab's own body so the panel behind shows through — the tab merges into the page. Hover means driving one hairline from alpha 51 to 255. Both are alpha animations on a single colour.

The recipe-book tabs use the classic ladder instead, and their selection works the other way — the fill lightens from slot-grey to panel-grey:

### 3.5 The tooltip

The famous frame is a **three-stop vertical gradient of one hue at a constant alpha**, over a near-black translucent fill. All four values are translucent; none of them is `FF`.

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `java.tooltip.background` | `#100010F0` | `J:sprites/tooltip/background.png` | 50,50 | fill — a near-black *purple*, at **alpha 240** |
| `java.tooltip.border_top` | `#5000FF50` | `J:sprites/tooltip/frame.png` | 50,9 | top stop, **alpha 80** |
| `java.tooltip.border_mid` | `#3C00BF50` | `J:sprites/tooltip/frame.png` | 9,50 | mid stop, alpha 80 |
| `java.tooltip.border_bottom` | `#28007F50` | `J:sprites/tooltip/frame.png` | 50,90 | bottom stop, alpha 80 |

Three things that only measurement gives you. The fill is `#100010` — it has a red and a blue component, it is not `#100000` or grey. Its alpha is 240, so the world dims through it rather than being hidden. And the border's three stops are exact halvings-and-a-bit of one hue: `50/3C/28` red, `FF/BF/7F` blue — the mid stop is the arithmetic mean of top and bottom in both channels, so a two-stop linear gradient from `#5000FF50` to `#28007F50` reproduces the frame exactly.

### 3.6 Text

| id | Hex | Source | (x, y) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `text.java.container_title` | `#3F3F3FFF` | `R:reference/inv-native.png` | 98,6 | container label ("Crafting", "Chest") |
| `text.java.container_title_crosscheck` | `#4A4A4AFF` | `R:reference/crafting-ui.png` | 896,144 | *lossy source*, cross-check only |
| `text.ore.primary` | `#FFFFFFFF` | `S:...Settings_Screen_Menu__General__Tab_(Bedrock).png` | 1380,307 | Ore UI body text on dark |
| `text.ore.secondary` | `#D0D1D4FF` | `S:...Settings_Screen_Menu__General__Tab_(Bedrock).png` | 1385,390 | Ore UI sub-label / description |
| `text.ore.on_light` | `#1E1E1FFF` | `S:...Settings_Screen_Menu__General__Tab_(Bedrock).png` | 1737,62 | Ore UI text on the light header |

The container title measured **`#3F3F3F`**, from a lossless 176×166 render whose text rect contains only two colours, so there is no compression ambiguity. The number quoted everywhere is `0x404040`. **One step apart, and the art is what ships** — recorded as measured, with the discrepancy noted in the JSON rather than reconciled. Grepping the repo for both `404040` and `3F3F3F` found no source-code match, so this colour is baked into art in our build and has no constant to disagree with.

**The shadow rule is `rgb >> 2` per channel, drawn at offset (+1, +1).** Documented, not measured, but it verifies exactly against the wiki's own background column: 255 → 63, 170 → 42, 85 → 21. That means white text casts `#3F3F3F` — the same value as the container title, which is a coincidence worth knowing but not a derivation, since the title is drawn without a shadow.

The sixteen formatting codes (`text.code.0` … `text.code.f`) are documented from `https://minecraft.wiki/w/Formatting_codes` and marked `measured: false` in the JSON. **Two of them cross-check against measured art exactly**: `§7 gray` = `#AAAAAA` is the button's upper bevel, and `§8 dark_gray` = `#555555` is the panel's lower bevel. That agreement is the reason to trust the other fourteen. The palette is the six-step ramp `00 / 55 / AA / FF` in each channel: `#000000`, `#0000AA`, `#00AA00`, `#00AAAA`, `#AA0000`, `#AA00AA`, `#FFAA00`, `#AAAAAA`, `#555555`, `#5555FF`, `#55FF55`, `#55FFFF`, `#FF5555`, `#FF55FF`, `#FFFF55`, `#FFFFFF`. Bedrock's `§7` is `#C6C6C6` rather than `#AAAAAA` — **the one place where the two languages disagree on a shared name**, and another reason not to merge them.

### 3.9 The bevel recipe

This is the part to keep. Given a fill, these are the exact values on each edge, in the reference's own numbers.

**Rule 1 — the classic bevel is three rungs off one six-rung ladder, and the direction of travel is the whole effect.** The ladder, dark to light: `#000000` · `#373737` · `#555555` · `#8B8B8B` · `#C6C6C6` · `#FFFFFF`. Nothing in the classic GUI invents a grey outside it except the hotbar frame, the scroller thumb and the disabled-slot corner.

**Raised — the panel.** Read outward-in from the top-left:

```
1px  #000000   border, all four sides
2px  #FFFFFF   highlight, TOP and LEFT only
n    #C6C6C6   fill
2px  #555555   shadow, BOTTOM and RIGHT only
1px  #000000   border
```
Corners are notched 2–3px fully transparent (`#00000000`). The highlight and shadow are **two** pixels wide.

**Sunken — the slot.** The same idea with the ladder walked the other way, and one pixel instead of two:

```
1px  #373737   shadow, TOP and LEFT
n    #8B8B8B   fill
1px  #FFFFFF   highlight, BOTTOM and RIGHT
     #8B8B8B   at the top-right and bottom-left corners — the FILL, not either bevel
```

Those two recipes are the same gesture in opposite directions: light-at-top-left means raised, dark-at-top-left means sunk. Note that the slot's contrast is *wider* than the panel's — it spans `#373737`→`#FFFFFF` across a `#8B8B8B` fill, while the panel spans `#555555`→`#FFFFFF` across `#C6C6C6`. A sunken cell is drawn harder than a raised panel, deliberately.

**Filled-in — the disabled slot.** Raised direction, but the fill climbs a rung so the cell reads as blocked rather than empty:

```
1px  #FFFFFF   TOP and LEFT
n    #C6C6C6   fill
1px  #8B8B8B   BOTTOM and RIGHT
     #B2B2B2   at the off-diagonal corners
```

**The button.** Four values, and the bevel is one pixel on all sides inside the outline:

```
1px  #000000   outline   (hover: #FFFFFF)
1px  #AAAAAA   TOP and LEFT   (hover: #AFAFAF)
n    #6F6F6F   body, dithered across 22 greys, mode 41.1%   (hover: #757575)
1px  #565656   BOTTOM and RIGHT   (hover: #5C5C5C)
```
**Hover = +6 per channel on the body and lower bevel, +5 on the upper, and the outline flips to white.** The dither pattern underneath is unchanged. **Disabled = flat `#2C2C2C` with the black outline and no bevel at all.**

**Ore UI — raised.** A different geometry, and the counter-intuitive part is that **all four inner edges are lighter than the fill.** There is no dark side. The 3D comes entirely from a 2px "base lip" below the control:

```
1px  #1E1E1F   border, all round
1px  <bevel_top>      TOP and LEFT      lighter than fill
n    <fill>
1px  <bevel_bottom>   BOTTOM and RIGHT  also lighter than fill, but less so
2px  <base_lip>       a dark slab below the fill, before the border
1px  #1E1E1F   border
```

| Colourway | bevel_top | fill | bevel_bottom | base_lip |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| light | `#ECEDEE` | `#D0D1D4` | `#E3E3E5` | `#58585A` |
| green | `#639D52` | `#3C8527` | `#4F913C` | `#1D4D13` |
| red | `#D55E5E` | `#CA3636` | `#CF4A4A` | `#AD1D1D` |

If you take one thing from Ore UI, take that: **remove the base lip and the control goes flat**, however carefully the bevels are tuned.

**Ore UI — sunken.** Grooves and separators are one dark line directly above one light line, two rows total, no fill:

| Context | upper (dark) | lower (light) |
|---|---|---|
| on the content pane `#48494A` | `#333334` | `#5A5B5C` |
| on the nav rail `#313233` | `#1D1E1F` | `#454647` |

**Rule 2 — alpha is part of the recipe, not a finishing touch.** The values that would be silently wrong at `FF`: slot hover back `#FFFFFF` **a=96** and front `#FFFFFF` **a=32**; tooltip fill **a=240** and its whole border **a=80**; tab body **a=219**, tab edge **a=191**, tab hairline **a=51** rising to **255** on hover; hotbar cell `#272505` **a=186**; selection glow **a=174**. Seven of the classic language's most visible surfaces are translucent.

**Rule 3 — focus is monochrome in both languages.** Java flips an outline to `#FFFFFF`; Ore UI draws a 1px `#FFFFFF` underline inside the control. Neither has a coloured focus ring, and adding one is the fastest way to look like neither.

### 3.10 What did not hold up, what is not measured, and how to re-check

**Held up:** `#C6C6C6` as the panel grey — 40.5% of the container rect and identical across six containers.

**Did not hold up:**
- The container title is `#3F3F3F`, one below the universally-quoted `0x404040`.
- Bedrock's slot highlight is `#FEFEFE`, not `#FFFFFF`.
- The hotbar cell is neither black nor opaque.
- The uncraftable recipe cell's fill is grey and *darker* than the craftable one, not red.
- The Ore UI content pane is lighter than its navigation rail, and selection darkens rather than lightens.

**Not measured, and flagged as such in the JSON:** the sixteen `§` formatting codes and the `rgb >> 2` shadow rule (`measured: false`, documented from minecraft.wiki, two of them independently confirmed against measured art). **Flagged `lossy_source: true`:** the six Bedrock red-slot and lossy-crosscheck values, whose only available images are compressed.

**To re-check any value:** open the file named in its `source`, call `GetPixel` at its `at`, compare. Every `pixel`, `run_scan` and `histogram_mode` entry in `ui-palette.json` — 201 of the 221 — is exactly reproducible that way, and all 201 were confirmed after the file was written.

## 4. Cell and screen geometry

Everything below was **measured from a file on disk**, not recalled. The method was the same
throughout: open the PNG with `System.Drawing`, walk a row or a column, and report the runs of
constant colour. A slot announces itself as a 1-px `#373737` run, sixteen pixels of `#8B8B8B`,
and a 1-px `#FFFFFF` run; the *periodicity* of those runs gives the pitch and the *first* one
gives the origin. That is a derivation, and it is why the pitch below is a measurement rather
than an assumption.

Machine-readable twin: **`assets\ui\ui-screens.json`** — same numbers, same provenance fields,
in 1x GUI pixels.

Two conventions govern every number here and getting them wrong is the classic one-pixel bug:

- **All coordinates are relative to the panel's top-left**, never to the image file. Most
  legacy sheets are 256x256 with the panel drawn in the top-left corner, so both are recorded.
- **The default anchor is the *item area*** — the top-left of the 16x16 square an item is drawn
  in, which is what vanilla's `Slot.x` / `Slot.y` hold. The painted **frame** is one pixel up
  and left of that. Where a number could be either, both are given.

---

### 4.1 The slot cell

The unit everything else is built from. It is 18x18, but *how* it is 18x18 matters more than
the number.

| Property | Measured | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| Frame (painted box) | **18 x 18** | `gui/sprites/container/slot.png` — the whole file is one cell |
| Item area | **16 x 16** | same, the `#8B8B8B` interior |
| Item offset inside the frame | **+1, +1** | same |
| Grid pitch | **18 x 18** | derived from run periodicity, `gui/container/generic_54.png` row 26 |
| Gap between two item areas | **2** | 18 pitch − 16 item |
| Dark edge (top, left) | `#373737`, **17 px long** | `gui/sprites/container/slot.png` |
| Light edge (bottom, right) | `#FFFFFF`, **17 px long** | same |
| Corners (17,0) and (0,17) | `#8B8B8B` — **neither dark nor white** | same |
| Hover / hit box | 18 x 18 at item − (1,1) | code (`isHovering` expands the 16x16 by 1 each side) |
| Empty-slot icons | **16 x 16**, 31 of them | `gui/sprites/container/slot/*.png`, drawn at the item origin |
| Hover highlight | **24 x 24**, nine-slice border 4, drawn at item − (4,4) | `slot_highlight_back.png.mcmeta` |

**The two far corners are the whole trick.** A cell is not a closed box; it is a dark L and a
light L, each 17 long, that interlock with the neighbouring cells. Adjacent slots *share* their
bevel edge, which is exactly why the pitch equals the frame size — 18, not 19 or 20. A detector
that assumes a closed 18x18 outline finds nothing, and a renderer that draws a closed box
produces a grid one pixel wider per column than the reference.

**The well-known numbers held.** 18x18 with a 16x16 interior is right, on Java *and* on Bedrock
(see 4.7.1).

---

### 4.2 The panel frame, and where the famous "8" comes from

Every container background is the same plate.

| Band | Width | Colour | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Outer border | 1 | `#000000` | `gui/container/inventory.png` row 78, column 120 |
| Highlight | 2 | `#FFFFFF` | same |
| Plate | fill | `#C6C6C6` | same |
| Shadow (bottom, right) | 2 | `#555555` | same |
| Outer border (bottom, right) | 1 | `#000000` | same |

Content inset is therefore **3**. Between the inset and the first slot frame sit **4** more
pixels of bare plate:

```
0  1 2  3 4 5 6  7 ......... 24  25
K  W W  P P P P  D  <16 fill>  L      K=black  W=white  P=plate  D=#373737  L=#FFFFFF
```

So the first **frame** is at x = 7 and the first **item** at x = **8**. The famous 8 is not a
free choice — it is `3 + 4 + 1`, and the same 3-then-4 margin appears on the Bedrock card too.

---

### 4.3 Every container screen

Panel size first. **The panel is not the file**: 24 of the 26 sheets are 256x256 with the panel
in the top-left corner.

| Screen | File | File size | Panel | Provenance (measured how) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory | `inventory.png` | 256x256 | **176 x 166** | opaque bounding box |
| Crafting table | `crafting_table.png` | 256x256 | 176 x 166 | opaque bounding box |

### 4.4 The standard relationships

These are what make every screen feel like the same program. All three were **derived from
measurements and then checked against panels of six different heights.**

Let **H** be the panel height:

| Rule | Value | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| Player storage, first item row | **y = H − 82** | derived; verified on 7 panels below |
| Hotbar item row | **y = H − 24** | derived; = storage + 22 |
| "Inventory" label | **y = H − 94** | 12 above storage; matches `inventoryLabelY = imageHeight - 94` (code) |
| Gap between storage row 3 and the hotbar | **4** | 84 + 3x18 = 138, hotbar frame at 141 |
| Storage top to hotbar top | **58** | 3x18 + 4 |
| Player inventory x | **8** (beacon 36, villager 108, creative 9) | measured per sheet |

| H | Storage y | Hotbar y | Check | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 166 | 84 | 142 | 166−82=84, 166−24=142 | `inventory.png`, `shulker_box.png`, `villager.png` |
| 133 | 51 | 109 | 133−82=51, 133−24=109 | `hopper.png` |
| 222 | 140 | 198 | 222−82=140, 222−24=198 | `generic_54.png` |
| 219 | 137 | 195 | 219−82=137, 219−24=195 | `beacon.png` |
| 136 | 54 | 112 | 136−82=54, 136−24=112 | `tab_inventory.png` |
| 220 | 138 | 196 | ours, 220−82=138 | `assets\textures\hud.png` y=1125 |

Seven independent panels, one rule, no exceptions. **This is the constant to hold in your head:
the player's inventory is anchored to the *bottom* of the panel, not the top.** Design a screen
by choosing its height, and the bottom half places itself.

**The container's own slots then get whatever is left**, and the pattern is consistent: a
container's first row sits at **y = 18** (chest, shulker, horse, creative items), leaving
18 − 3 = 15 px of plate for the title. The gap between the container's last row and the player
storage is then whatever the height forced.

**Other constants that repeat:**

| Constant | Value | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| Result well | 26 x 26, interior 24 x 24, item centred at well + (5,5) | 5 sheets agree exactly |
| Progress arrow | 22 x 15 | 7 sheets |
| Plus sign | 13 x 13 | `anvil.png`, `cartography_table.png` |
| Recipe list well | 14 wide, interior 12 | `loom.png`, `stonecutter.png` |
| Title label | (8, 6), line height 9 | code |
| Panel centring | `leftPos = (guiScaledWidth − panelW) / 2`, integer | code |

The **26x26 result well** is worth spelling out because it is the one place the item is *not*
at frame + (1,1): the well is 26 outer, 24 interior, and the 16x16 item is centred in that
interior — item = well + (5,5). Verified independently on the crafting table (124,35), furnace
(116,35), stonecutter (143,33), cartography (145,39) and villager (220,37), all five matching
the known menu coordinates exactly.

> **One honest disagreement.** Applying the same centring to the loom's measured well
> (138,52) gives an item origin of **(143,57)**, while the loom's menu is commonly quoted at
> **(143,58)**. The texture is the owner of where the *well* is drawn; the menu is the owner of
> where the item is *hit-tested*. They differ by a pixel on this one screen. Published as
> measured, flagged rather than smoothed over.

Sizes measured from the sprite files; placement is code and is marked as such. Let
**C = guiScaledWidth / 2**, **W = guiScaledWidth**, **H = guiScaledHeight**.

| Element | Size | Placement | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hotbar | **182 x 22** | (C − 91, H − 22) | `sprites/hud/hotbar.png`; placement from code |
| Hotbar cell pitch | **20** | items at (C − 90 + 20i + 2, H − 19) | measured: 3 border + 9x16 + 8x4 + 3 = 182 |
| Hotbar item area | 16 x 16 at (3,3) in the sprite | — | `hotbar.png` run scan |
| Selector | **24 x 23** | (C − 92 + 20i, H − 23) | `hotbar_selection.png` |
| Selector hole | 16 x 16 at (4,4) | lands exactly on the cell | measured: fully transparent region |
| Crosshair | **15 x 15**, cross is 9x9 at (3,3) | ((W − 15)/2, (H − 15)/2) | `crosshair.png` |
| XP bar | **182 x 5** | ((W − 182)/2, H − 29) | `experience_bar_background.png` |
| XP progress width | `(int)(progress * 183)` | — | code |
| XP level text | — | y = H − 35 | code |
| Jump bar | 182 x 5 | same slot as the XP bar | `jump_bar_background.png` |
| Health / armour / food / air icons | **9 x 9** each | see below | `sprites/hud/heart/*`, `armor_*`, `food_*`, `air*` |
| Status row pitch | **8** horizontal, **10** vertical | left x = C − 91, right x = C + 91, base y = H − 39 | code |
| Effect background | 24 x 24 | top-right | `sprites/hud/effect_background.png` |
| Offhand slot | 29 x 24 | beside the hotbar | `hotbar_offhand_left/right.png` |
| Attack indicator (hotbar) | 18 x 18 | beside the hotbar | `hotbar_attack_indicator_*.png` |
| Attack indicator (crosshair) | 16 x 16 / 16 x 4 | under the crosshair | `crosshair_attack_indicator_*.png` |

**The hotbar is the one place the pitch is not 18.** It is **20**, because the hotbar's cells
are separated by a 4-px divider rather than sharing a 2-px bevel. Ten hearts likewise span 81
px, not 90, because the status icons are 9 wide on an 8 pitch — they deliberately overlap by a
pixel. Both are easy to get wrong by carrying the container's 18 across.

The hotbar's own width, **182**, is also the XP bar's width, which is why they line up: the
whole HUD hangs off `C ± 91`.

merges into the page below it. And the **recipe book's 25x25** is the one cell in the whole UI
that is not 18x18: it is a button that happens to contain an item, not a slot.

scanning every row of the sheet for its opaque extent.

| Strip | y | Height | Width | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Widgets | 0 | 41 | 185 | row-extent scan of `hud.png` |
| Inventory | 41 | 166 | 176 | same |
| Crafting | 207 | 166 | 176 | same |
| Furnace | 373 | 166 | 176 | same |
| Book card | 555 | 166 | 146 | same |
| Tabs (5 x 22x25, pitch 24, selected at +27) | 721 | 52 | 118 | same; 4x24 + 22 = 118 |
| Cells (4 states, 18x18, pitch 20) | 773 | 18 | 78 | same; 3x20 + 18 = 78 |
| Smithing | 793 | 166 | 176 | same |

| Hopper | 1355 | 166 | 176 | same |
| Stonecutter | 1521 | 166 | 176 | same |

**Our panel frame is byte-identical to the reference's** — 1 black, 2 white, `#C6C6C6`, 2
`#555555`, 1 black, content inset 3, first frame at 7, first item at 8. Our cell is 18x18 with
a 16x16 interior. So is our pitch.

Where ours diverges:

| Screen | Ours | Reference | Delta | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory (all six regions) | 8,8 / 98,18 / 154,28 / 77,62 / 8,84 / 8,142 | identical | **none** | `hud.png` y=41 vs `inventory.png` |
| Crafting grid | 29, 17 | 30, 17 | **1 px left** | `hud.png` y=207 |
| Crafting result | 123, 35 (plain 18x18) | 124, 35 (26x26 well) | 1 px left, **no well** | same |
| Furnace input / fuel | 55, 17 / 55, 53 | 56, 17 / 56, 53 | **1 px left** | `hud.png` y=373 |
| Furnace result | 115, 35 (plain) | 116, 35 (well) | 1 px left, **no well** | same |
| Smithing | 2 inputs at 37,35 & 55,35; result 123,35 | 3 inputs at 8/26/44, y=48; result 98,48 | **different screen** | `hud.png` y=793 |
| Chest (3 rows) | 176x166, container 8,18, storage 8,84 | `shulker_box.png` identical | **none** | `hud.png` y=959 |
| Double chest | 176 x **220**, storage 138, hotbar 196 | 176 x **222**, storage 140, hotbar 198 | **2 px shorter** | `hud.png` y=1125 |
| Hopper | 176 x **166**, row at 44,35 | 176 x **133**, row at 44,20 | **33 px taller** | `hud.png` y=1355 |
| Stonecutter | input 20,35; three fixed cuts at 86/104/122, y=35 | input 20,33; scrolling 12x54 list at 119,15; 26x26 well | **different mechanism** | `hud.png` y=1521 |
| Book card | 146 x 166, content area 140x160 at (3,3) | — (ours alone) | — | `hud.png` y=555 |

Three of these are deliberate design (smithing, stonecutter, the book card). Three are not:

1. **The 1-px left shift** on the crafting grid and the furnace column. `tools\make-hud-sheet.ps1`
   carries a comment justifying it: *"our slot borders sit at x 7, 25, 43 … where the reference's
   sit at 8, 26, 44."* **Both are the same cells.** 7/25/43 are *frame* origins and 8/26/44 are
   *item* origins — the reference's frames are also at 7, 25, 43. The comment compares two
   different anchors, and the shift it justifies is real but unnecessary. Our storage rows, which
   were not shifted, match the reference exactly, which is the proof. Recorded, not fixed — this
   work does not edit source.
2. **Our double chest is 2 px short** (220 vs 222). Our own H−82 / H−24 rule still holds
   internally, so nothing looks wrong; it just will not overlay the reference.
3. **We have no 26x26 result well.** Every reference craft-like screen emphasises its output
   with a bigger recess; ours uses a plain cell, so our outputs read as "just another slot."

#### 4.7.1 The two-card layout, against Bedrock

`INTERFACE.md` §5.7 measures our design at 3x. The Bedrock crops in `reference\ui-icons\` let
that be checked at 1x.

| Measurement | Ours (`INTERFACE.md` / `hud.png`) | Bedrock (`ui-icons`) | Provenance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Left (catalogue) card width | **146** | **146** | `card-left-full.png`, panel x 1..146 |
| Left card height | 166 | ~190 | `card-left-full.png`, panel y 1..190 |
| Right (inventory) card width | **176** | **176** | `card-right-full.png`, panel x 1..176 |
| Right card height | 166 | ~167 | `card-right-full.png` |
| Gap between cards | 4 | — | `INTERFACE.md` §5.7 |
| Total block width | **326** | — | 146 + 4 + 176 |
| Slot pitch | 18 | **18** | `card-right-full.png` row 113 |
| First item x | 8 | **8** | same row: dark edges at 8, 26, 44, 62, 80, 98, 116, 134, 152 |
| Left margin | 3 border + 4 plate | 3 border + 4 plate | same |
| Tab | 22 x 25, pitch 24 | 22 x 25 | `hud.png` y=721 vs `tab-*.png` |
| Scrollbar | — | 15 x 133 | `scrollbar.png` |
| Empty slot | 18 x 18 | 18 x 18 | `slot-empty.png` (and 54x54 at 3x) |

**Our widths are already right.** Both cards match Bedrock exactly, and Bedrock's inventory
card uses the same cell, the same pitch and the same left margin as Java — which is the single
most useful cross-check in this whole document, because it means one geometry serves both
references. Where we differ is **height**: our catalogue card is 166 where Bedrock's is ~190,
so ours shows fewer rows for the same cell size.

Two cautions on the `ui-icons` numbers. They are crops out of a screenshot, so each carries one
or two pixels of surrounding screen — the *widths* are exact because the black border pixel is
unambiguous, the *heights* carry ±1. And `slot-empty.png`'s bevel phase is shifted a pixel
(light at x=0, dark at x=1), which is a crop offset, not a different cell; the 3x file confirms
3-px edges = 1 unit.

One correction while here: **`layout-book-inventory.png` and `layout-inventory-only.png` are
not layout diagrams.** They are the two Bedrock layout-toggle *button glyphs*, 29x19 and 27x19.

### 4.8 What the reference does not tell you

Three things had to be marked "code" rather than "measured", and it is worth being explicit
about which, so nobody later mistakes them for measurements:

| Value | Why it is not measurable | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Horse saddle / armour slots (8,18) and (8,36) | Not drawn on `horse.png` in 26.2 — blitted from `slot.png` at runtime | code |
| Every label position | Text is not in the texture | code |
| All HUD placement rules | Sprites are positioned by the renderer | code |
| Tooltip offsets | Same | code |
| Chest row formula | Only the 6-row sheet exists | derived from the 6-row sheet, cross-checked against code |

The chest formula deserves a note. `panel_height = 114 + rows * 18` reproduces the measured
222 for 6 rows, and `storage_y = rows * 18 + 32` reproduces 140. But the commonly quoted code
listing blits `rows*18 + 17` pixels for the top section, and that lands one pixel short of what
`generic_54.png` actually contains; the measured texture is reproduced by `rows*18 + 18`
followed by the `v=126, h=96` strip. **The texture is the owner.** And `shulker_box.png` is a
measured 176x166 with storage at 84 — two pixels shorter than the formula's 168/86 for the same
three rows — so the shulker screen must not be generated from the chest rule.

---

### 4.9 GUI scale

Not measurable from an image; researched and cited. The algorithm has been unchanged from
1.20.1 through 26.2.

```
scale = 1
while (scale != maxScale
       && scale < framebufferWidth && scale < framebufferHeight
       && framebufferWidth  / (scale + 1) >= 320
       && framebufferHeight / (scale + 1) >= 240)
    scale++
if (enforceUnicode && scale % 2 != 0) scale++
```

| Constant | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `BASE_WIDTH` | **320** | the loop refuses a scale that would leave less than this |
| `BASE_HEIGHT` | **240** | same |
| GUI Scale "Auto" | 0 | means maxScale unclamped — the loop runs until the 320x240 test fails |
| `guiScaledWidth` | `ceil(framebufferWidth / scale)` | |
| `guiScaledHeight` | `ceil(framebufferHeight / scale)` | |
| Panel centring | `leftPos = (guiScaledWidth − panelW) / 2`, integer | so a panel can land on a half-pixel of the framebuffer, never of the GUI grid |

Sources: `Window.calculateScale` in the Mojang-mapped decompilation (mirrored on the usual
decompilation sites), and minecraft.wiki's *Options* page for the user-facing behaviour.

**Two corrections to widely repeated claims.** First, a hard **320x240 minimum window size** is
a **26.3** change that arrived with the SDL3 switch — it is not a long-standing 1.13 feature;
before that, 320x240 was only the auto-scale loop's floor. Second, **Bedrock does not use this
loop at all** — its GUI scale is a *percentage* modifier on a computed base, which is why a
Bedrock screenshot can sit at a non-integer factor and why our `ui-icons` crops needed a 3x set
to verify against.

**What this means for us:** everything in this document is an integer number of GUI pixels
multiplied by an integer scale. Pixel-exactness is achievable, and the only way to lose it is
to compute a layout in floats or to centre something with a non-integer divide.

---

### The rules of thumb

The handful that, once known, get a new screen right first time.

1. **The cell is 18, the item is 16, the item sits at +1,+1, and the pitch is 18.** Slots share
   their bevel; a grid of N columns is `N*18` wide, not `N*18 + 1`.
2. **The panel margin is 3 + 4.** Three pixels of border (1 black, 2 white), four of bare
   plate. First frame at 7, first **item at 8**. That is the entire reason x = 8 is everywhere.
3. **The bottom of the panel is the anchor, not the top.** Player storage at **H − 82**, hotbar
   at **H − 24**, the "Inventory" label at **H − 94**. Choose your panel height and the bottom
   half places itself. Verified on seven panels from 133 to 222 tall.
4. **The container's own first row is at y = 18**, leaving 15 px of plate for the title, which
   sits at **(8, 6)** with a 9-px line height.
5. **176 x 166 is the default, not the rule.** Hopper 176x133, chest `114 + rows*18`, villager
   276x166, beacon 230x219, creative 195x136. Five of twenty-six diverge — always measure.
6. **A result slot is emphasised with a 26x26 well**, interior 24x24, item centred at well +
   (5,5). A plain 18x18 output looks like an input.
7. **The progress arrow is 22 x 15.** Same on seven screens. The plus is 13x13, the flame 14x14.
8. **The HUD does not use 18.** The hotbar pitch is **20** (4-px dividers), the status icons are
   9 wide on an **8** pitch (they overlap), and everything hangs off `centreX ± 91` because the
   hotbar and the XP bar are both **182** wide.
9. **Read nine-slice borders from the `.mcmeta`, never from the image.** Button 3, text field
   and slider 1, tab `b0`, tooltip background 9 and frame 10.
10. **Say which anchor you mean, every time.** Frame or item — they differ by one pixel, and the
    only bug in our own panels that is not a design choice was caused by comparing one against
    the other.

---

## 5. The screens we do not have

Everything outside the world is 0 % built. There is no main menu, no world list, no world
creation, no pause, no settings screen and no death screen — confirmed by reading the code
rather than by re-reading `GAPS.md`: the only screen state in the whole program is
`std::optional<game::inventoryScreen::Kind> openScreen;` at `game/src/Main.cpp:2562`, and
`Escape` at `Main.cpp:3199-3208` either closes that or releases the mouse and does nothing
else. The seed is `constexpr std::uint32_t kWorldSeed = 1337u;` (`Main.cpp:171`), so a new
world is a recompile. 44 keys are parsed by `core/Settings.cpp` and none is reachable from a
screen; 12 further actions are spread across 16 undocumented function keys.

This section specifies those screens precisely enough to build them. **It does not build
them and it does not re-report that they are missing.** Five other agents cover the existing
UI code, the sprite atlas, the palette, cell geometry and the in-world HUD; where this
section needs one of those it names the existing symbol and stops.

**Two things must be settled before any of it, and §5.1 and §5.2 settle them.**

---

### 5.1 The decision: classic, not Ore UI

**Classic.** Every out-of-world screen is built from the vanilla widget set — the 200 × 20
nine-sliced button, the 200 × 20 slider with its 8 × 20 handle, the 200 × 20 text field, the
130 × 24 tab, the 6 × 32 scroller — drawn in the same six greys and the same raised/recessed
bevel logic the inventory already uses (`INTERFACE.md §5.1-5.3`), over a tiled, darkened
dirt background.

Three sentences of argument, as asked:

1. **We already draw exactly this.** The container screens are the classic look, our art
   pipeline stages classic sprites, our palette is the classic six greys, and our text
   renderer is the classic 8 px proportional font — choosing Ore UI would mean carrying two
   incompatible visual systems in one program and authoring a second art pipeline for the
   half that is not built yet, which is the opposite of *"heavily utilize what we already
   have"*.
2. **The reference's own settings screens are classic where it counts.** `Vibrant_Visuals_menu.png`
   — the newest graphics screen Mojang ships, and the one closest to what our renderer
   exposes — is a plain vertical list of `Label: Value` sliders in classic greys, not a card
   grid; `Pause_Menu_(Bedrock_26.0).png` is four stacked light-grey buttons over a blurred
   world. Bedrock's Ore UI shell wraps a classic interior, so following the classic interior
   is *not* a departure from Bedrock-as-reference.
3. **Ore UI's cost is all in the parts we do not need.** Its flat dark cards, teal accents,
   left-hand icon rail and panorama exist to organise Realms, Marketplace, friends,
   achievements and sign-in; strip those (§5.2) and roughly four fifths of the layout has
   nothing to hold, leaving an expensive shell around five sliders.

**What we take from Ore UI anyway,** because it is better and costs nothing: the
*row* shape of a settings entry — bold label left, one-line grey description under it,
control right-aligned on the same row (`Ore_UI_-_Settings_Screen_Menu__Video__Tab_(Bedrock).png`).
A description line under each option is the single largest usability difference between the
two systems and it is one extra `appendText` call. Vanilla Java's options screen has no
description line and is worse for it.

**And one thing we do not take:** the accent colour. Ore UI's green (`#3C8527`) marks the
selected item in a segmented control. We already have a red/green cell-state vocabulary in
the catalogue (`INTERFACE.md §3.1`); menus stay monochrome except for the destructive-action
red in §5.10, so that red keeps its meaning.

#### 5.1.1 The geometry vocabulary

Everything below is stated in **art pixels**, the unit the inventory already uses:

```
kPixel = kPanelHeight / kPanelPixelSize.y = 1.30f / 166.0f = 0.00783133 screen units
        — InventoryScreen.cpp:147, :65, :155
```

Screen space is −1..1 over the window **height** on both axes with X divided by aspect in
the renderer (`Renderer.hpp:105-112`), so:

| | Screen units | Art pixels |
|---|---|---|
| Screen height, every window | 2.0 | **255.4** |
| Screen width at 16:9 | 3.556 | **454.0** |
| Screen width at 4:3 | 2.667 | **340.5** |
| Screen width at 21:9 | 4.667 | **595.9** |
| Screen width at 1.28:1 (the aspect §2.4 flags) | 2.560 | **326.9** |

A vanilla 200 px button is therefore **44 % of the width at 16:9** — inside the 31–50 % band
vanilla itself spans across its GUI scales, so the reference's proportions transfer without
rescaling. **Reuse `kPixel`; do not introduce a second art-pixel constant** (bug shape #1:
a value derived somewhere other than the one table that owns it). Promote it out of
`InventoryScreen.cpp` into `hud/HudPrimitives.hpp` beside `kSheetSize` so both owners read
one definition, and `static_assert(kPixel * 166.0f == 1.30f)`.

**Resize rule, one sentence, applied to every screen in this section:** art pixels are a
fixed fraction of window *height*, so nothing reflows on resize — screens are centred on
(0, 0), lists change **row count** and never row size, and the only element that tracks
aspect is the full-bleed background. The widest element anywhere below is 220 art px
(= 1.723 screen units), which needs aspect ≥ 0.862; the narrow-aspect clipping recorded in
`GAPS.md §2.4` cannot recur here, and every screen must state its widest element so that
stays true.

#### 5.1.2 The sprite sheet has to widen once

The HUD sheet is `185 × 1687` px and is asserted at that size at `Main.cpp:1776-1792`. The
widest new art is the 200 px button and the 256 px title wordmark, so **the sheet widens to
256 px**. This is cheap and safe: `appendSprite` normalises by the `sheetSize` argument
(`HudPrimitives.cpp:62`), every caller passes `hud::kSheetSize`, and existing content keeps
its pixel coordinates — so changing `kSheetSize` (`HudPrimitives.hpp:24`) plus the canvas
width in `tools/make-hud-sheet.ps1` and `tools/make-reference-hud.ps1` is the entire change
and no existing rect moves. Do it once, in the shared slice (§5.3), not per screen.

Source art for the staging scripts, all already on disk:
`reference/minecraft-assets-26.2/minecraft-assets-26.2/assets/minecraft/textures/gui/sprites/widget/*.png`
(50 files, 16 with `.png.mcmeta` nine-slice metadata) and
`.../textures/gui/title/minecraft.png` (1024 × 256).

---

### 5.2 What is cut, permanently — write this down so nobody rebuilds a store

This is a single-player, personal-use game. The following are **cut, not deferred**, and a
future session that finds a gap here should close the tab rather than fill it:

| Cut | Where it appears in the reference | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Realms — create, join, manage, subscriptions, stories, invite links | ~30 of the 131 screenshots on disk | Multiplayer is permanently cut (`CLAUDE.md`) |
| Marketplace, DLC, Marketplace Pass, Character Creator, Dressing Room | `Marketplace*.png`, `AMCM_DLC_Purchase_Screen.png`, `Character_Creator.png` | Personal build, no store, one skin |
| Sign-in, accounts, profile, friends, followers, party, social drawer, player permissions, report behaviour, inbox/news | `Ore_UI_-_Sign_In_*`, `*Profile*`, `*Social*`, `*Player_Permissions*`, `*Inbox*` | No accounts exist |
| Achievements and the "you can't earn achievements" nags | `Ore_UI_-_Achievements_*` | `GAPS.md` G2.20, XL, no system behind it |
| Resource packs, behaviour packs, global resources, add-ons, experiments, world templates | the create-world tab family | One asset set, compiled in |
| Multiplayer / LAN / servers tabs, world import and export, world thumbnails from screenshots | `Ore_UI_-_Play_Screen_Menu__Servers__*`, `*Import_World*`, `*Select_Screenshot*` | No networking, no screenshot capture |
| Touch controls tab, storage tab, subscriptions tab, language tab | `Ore_UI_-_Settings_Screen_Menu__Touch__Tab_*`, `BE_Storage_settings.png`, `*Language*` | No touch device, no store, English only |
| Nether/End anything | — | Out of scope by instruction |

**What survives is four verbs: start, resume, configure, quit.** Everything specified below
serves one of them.

Two things Bedrock has that we *do* keep, and should not be mistaken for scope creep because
they close named gaps: a **How to Play / Controls page** (`Bedrock_How_to_Play_button_(pause_menu).png`),
because 16 undocumented function keys is the problem it solves; and **Enable Game Pause**
behaviour (visible in `Ore_UI_-_Settings_Screen_Menu__General__Tab_(Bedrock).png` —
*"A single-player feature that pauses gameplay while the game menu is open"*), because we
are single-player-only and therefore always on the side of that toggle where it works.

---

### 5.3 The shared layer — screen stack, focus, widgets, text input

**This is the real work; the screens are cheap afterwards.** Every subsection from §5.4 on
assumes this exists and refers to it by name. Build it first, as one slice, and build nothing
screen-shaped until it draws a button that highlights under the pointer and under a gamepad.

#### 5.3.0 Prerequisite: `engine::Key` is missing everything a menu needs

`engine/include/engine/platform/Window.hpp:22-59` defines exactly: `W A S D E F G C V Q
Space LeftShift LeftControl Escape Num1..Num9 F1..F12 Backspace Enter`. **There are no
arrow keys, no `Tab`, no `Delete`, no `Home`/`End`.** Menu focus movement, slider
adjustment and text-caret editing are all impossible until they are added.

Add: `Left, Right, Up, Down, Tab, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown`. Keep `Num1..Num9`
contiguous (the comment at `Window.hpp:36-37` says game code maps a hotbar slot by
subtracting `Num1`). **XS, and it blocks every other item in this section.**

#### 5.3.1 App mode and the shape of `main()`

`main()` is one 6,722-line straight-line function (`Main.cpp:978`) whose ~4,000-line frame
loop closes over ~100 locals. A menu that runs *without a world* cannot live inside it.

The minimum honest split — and deliberately not a state-machine rewrite:

```
enum class AppMode { Menu, Playing, Quit };
enum class ExitReason { ToTitle, QuitApp };

struct WorldChoice { std::filesystem::path directory; };   // resolved by §5.5 / §5.6

ExitReason runMenus(Ctx&);                    // owns §5.4, §5.5, §5.6
ExitReason playWorld(Ctx&, const WorldChoice&);  // the current frame loop, hoisted
```

`Ctx` holds what must outlive both and is expensive to build: `Window` (`Main.cpp:1006`,
"only one Window may exist at a time"), `VulkanContext` (`:1007`), `Renderer` (`:1814` — takes
the block, HUD and font atlases as constructor arguments and has **no re-upload path**),
`JobSystem` (`:996`), `AudioEngine` + `Sounds` (`:1000-1004`), the font advance table
(`:1833-1859`) and `Settings`. `World` is constructed **inside** `playWorld` and destroyed on
return, which is what makes "Save and Quit to Title" possible at all.

Consequences to plan for, each a real edit:

- `window.setCursorCaptured(true)` at `Main.cpp:1893` fires before the first frame; it moves
  into `playWorld` and the menu path holds the cursor free.
- The loading loop at `Main.cpp:2043-2101` is already a self-contained screen-only frame loop
  (poll → `setScreenMesh` → `drawFrame`). **It is the template for the menu loop** — copy its
  shape rather than inventing one.
- `JobSystem jobs(settings.workerThreads)` is sized once at `:996`. That is why
  `worker_threads` is the one setting marked *restart* in §5.8.
- The shutdown save block at `Main.cpp:7033-7100` becomes `void saveEverything(...)` so that
  "Save and Quit" and window-close call the same code. Today the game **only** saves on
  window close — there is no autosave — so this refactor is also the first crash-safety the
  project gets.

#### 5.3.2 The screen stack

```
enum class ScreenId : std::uint8_t {
    MainMenu, WorldSelect, WorldCreate, Pause, Settings, HowToPlay, Death, Confirm,
    Container,      // the existing inventoryScreen::Kind family, as the leaf
};

constexpr std::size_t kMaxScreenDepth = 4;   // Pause → Settings → Confirm is the deepest real path
```

Rules:

- `push(id)`, `pop()`, `replace(id)`, `clear()`. `top()` receives input. Everything below
  `top()` still **draws** (that is what makes a modal read as modal) and receives nothing.
- **Escape / B pops.** At depth 1 in `Playing`, popping means resume. At depth 1 in `Menu`,
  `MainMenu` is the floor and Escape does nothing (Quit is a button, never a keystroke —
  losing a world to a stray Escape is unacceptable).
- The existing `openScreen` optional (`Main.cpp:2562`) becomes `ScreenId::Container` plus its
  `Kind`; `closeScreen` (`Main.cpp:2790-2827`) becomes the `Container` pop handler and keeps
  every one of its current duties (give back `heldStack`, give back the craft grid, play
  `SoundEvent::ChestClose`, `hudDirty = true`). **Do not let a second copy of that logic
  appear** — bug shape #14, a rule that did not travel.
- Opening any menu screen while a container screen is open first pops the container, so the
  held stack is never stranded.
- **Depth.** Every menu quad is blended and a blended fragment still writes depth (bug shape
  #6), so depth must be strictly ordered and nothing overlapping may share one.
  `kScreenDepthBase = 0.0044f`, `kScreenDepthStep = 0.0010f`; stack level *n* occupies
  `[base − n·step, base − n·step − 0.0009f]` with 9 sub-bands of `0.0001f` inside it
  (background, panel, widget body, widget bevel, label, value, focus ring, tooltip, pointer).
  Level 0 = 0.0044 exactly matches the inventory's existing `kDimDepth`
  (`InventoryScreen.cpp:21-42`), so the two systems interleave without a new range.
- **Which mesh layer.** All three exist already: `setScreenMesh` (`Renderer.hpp:107`) for the
  background and static widgets, `setClippedScreenMesh` (`:121`, scissor at `Renderer.cpp:2216`)
  for the one scrolling list a screen may have, `setTopScreenMesh` (`:131`) for the pointer,
  tooltips and any modal above a scroll region.
- **Rebuild policy.** Menus rebuild their mesh on any input event, on a hover change, and
  while a slider is being dragged — never unconditionally per frame. Mirror the existing
  `hudDirty` flag with `screenDirty`.

#### 5.3.3 The focus model

One struct, one flag, and the rule that makes pad and mouse coexist:

```
struct Focus { int index = 0; bool visible = false; };
```

- Each screen exposes an ordered, fixed array of widgets. `Focus::index` indexes the
  **enabled and focusable** subset; disabled widgets are skipped by movement and cannot be
  activated.
- **Moving the mouse shows the pointer and sets `visible = false`. Any directional keyboard
  or pad input hides the pointer and sets `visible = true`.** Drive this from the existing
  `resolveInputDevice(InputMode, InputDevice, const Gamepad&, bool keyboardActive)`
  (`core/Gamepad.hpp:145`) so it obeys `input_mode` (Auto / Keyboard / Gamepad, cycled by `F`
  today) rather than inventing a second notion of "which device is driving".
- **Hovering also sets `Focus::index`**, so Enter after a hover activates the obvious thing.
- Focus ring: a 1 art px white outline inset −2 px around the widget rect, four
  `appendQuad` strips at the focus sub-band. Drawn **in addition to** the `_highlighted`
  sprite, because a pad user must be able to tell focus from a stale hover.
- Every screen below names its **default focus** explicitly. Never leave it at index 0 by
  accident when index 0 is destructive.

#### 5.3.4 Navigation, exhaustively

| Action | Keyboard | Mouse | Gamepad |
|---|---|---|---|
| Move focus | `Up`/`Down`, `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` | hover | D-pad up/down, left stick (magnitude ≥ 0.5, 4-way) |
| Adjust slider / cycler | `Left`/`Right` (`Shift` = ×5 step) | drag handle, or click track to jump; wheel over the row = ±1 step | D-pad left/right, left stick left/right |
| Activate | `Enter` or `Space` | left click (press *and* release inside the widget) | `A` |
| Back / cancel / pop | `Escape` | click the 14 × 14 cross button, top-right | `B` |
| Change tab | `PageUp`/`PageDown` | click the tab | `LB`/`RB` — already the inventory's binding (`Main.cpp:3391-3400`) |
| Scroll a list | `PageUp`/`PageDown`, `Home`/`End` | wheel, or drag the scroller | right stick Y, or D-pad at the list edge |
| Text caret | `Left`/`Right`/`Home`/`End`, `Backspace`, `Delete` | click to place caret | on-screen keyboard is **out of scope**; a pad focusing a text field shows the hint *"Use the keyboard to type"* |

Repeat timing for held directions reuses the pad's existing values so both devices feel the
same: `kRepeatDelaySeconds = 0.4f`, `kRepeatIntervalSeconds = 0.11f` (`core/Gamepad.cpp:8-45`),
and `pad.repeated(PadButton)` already implements it. **The D-pad is currently bound to
nothing in `Main.cpp`** — it is free.

The gamepad virtual pointer (`Gamepad::pointerDelta`, integrated at `Main.cpp:3126-3131`)
stays available on every screen and is simply hidden while the focus ring is up. It is the
fallback for anything the focus order cannot reach, and it is already built.

#### 5.3.5 The widget set — seven kinds, real sizes

Sizes and nine-slice borders are read from the reference sprites and their `.mcmeta`, not
invented:

| Widget | Sprite | Size (art px) | Nine-slice border | States |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Button | `widget/button` | 200 × 20 | 3 | normal, `button_highlighted` (hover/focus), pressed, `button_disabled` (border 1) |
| Small button | same, nine-sliced narrower | 98 × 20 | 3 | two fit a 200 column with a 4 px gap |
| Icon button | `widget/cross_button` | 14 × 14 | — | normal, `_highlighted` |
| Slider | `widget/slider` + `slider_handle` | 200 × 20 track, 8 × 20 handle | 1 / L2 T2 R2 B3 | track normal + `_highlighted`; handle normal + `_highlighted` |
| Text field | `widget/text_field` | 200 × 20 | 1 | normal, `_highlighted` (focused) |
| Tab | `widget/tab` | 130 × 24, drawn narrower | L2 T2 R2 B0 | `tab`, `tab_highlighted`, `tab_selected`, `tab_selected_highlighted` |
| Scrollbar | `widget/scroller_background` + `scroller` | 6 × 32 each | 1 | thumb min length 16 px |

**Booleans and enums are cyclers, not checkboxes.** A cycler is a Button whose label is
`"Bloom: On"` / `"Shadows: Medium"` / `"Clouds: Fancy"` — vanilla's own mechanism, no extra
art, one code path shared with Button, and it reads correctly at 8 px where a 20 × 20
checkbox does not. The 20 × 20 `checkbox` sprites are staged anyway and left unused; if a
future session wants Bedrock's toggle look, the art is there. This collapses `GAPS.md §2.2`'s
"three widget kinds" to **two value widgets (slider, cycler) plus the button they share**,
which covers 42 of the 44 settings keys; the remaining two are the text fields in §5.6.

Text colours, from vanilla and consistent with `INTERFACE.md §5.1`:

| Role | RGBA |
|---|---|
| Label, normal | `{1.00, 1.00, 1.00, 1}` with shadow |
| Label, hovered/focused | `{1.00, 1.00, 0.63, 1}` (255,255,160) |
| Label, disabled | `{0.63, 0.63, 0.63, 1}` (160,160,160), no shadow |
| Description line | `{0.63, 0.63, 0.63, 1}` at 6 px |
| Value / units | `{0.78, 0.78, 0.78, 1}` |
| Destructive | `{0.85, 0.25, 0.25, 1}` tint on the button sprite |
| Restart-required marker | `{1.00, 0.67, 0.25, 1}` |

Hit-testing keeps the existing immediate-mode point-in-rect model (`slotAt`, `tabAt`,
`insideSearchField` in `InventoryScreen.cpp`); do not introduce retained widget objects.
**Press must be press-and-release inside the same widget** — today's clicks are bare edge
events from `window.consumeMouseButtonPresses()` (`Main.cpp:3448`), which is fine for slots
and wrong for a Delete button.

#### 5.3.6 The new primitives

Four functions, all in `hud/HudPrimitives.*` beside the existing ten. Nothing else new is
needed anywhere in this section.

1. **`appendNineSlice(MeshData&, rect, depth, pixelMin, pixelSize, border, sheetSize, tint)`**
   — ~40 lines, nine `appendSprite` calls with zero-size pieces skipped, accepting either a
   scalar border or `{left, top, right, bottom}`. **This is the single highest-value new
   primitive in the whole section**: it makes buttons, sliders, text fields, tabs and
   scrollbars resizable from one 200 × 20 source each. Today there is no nine-slice and no
   bevel routine at all — the inventory draws whole panels as single sprites
   (`InventoryScreen.cpp:723-724`).
2. **`appendTextCentred` / `appendTextRight`** — trivial wrappers over the existing
   `appendText` + `textWidth` (`HudPrimitives.cpp:247`, `:234`). Every caller centres by hand
   today (`LoadingScreen.cpp:53-54`); that is four screens' worth of duplicated arithmetic
   waiting to disagree.
3. **`wrapText(std::string_view, float maxWidth, float charHeight) -> small_vector<std::string_view>`**
   — greedy break on spaces, hard break on a word longer than the line. Required by every
   settings description line and by §5.10. Does not exist.
4. **`appendTextEllipsised(..., float maxWidth)`** — for world names longer than the row.

Plus one background helper, `appendTiledBackground(MeshData&, BlockId, float tilePixels = 32,
vec4 tint = {0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 1})`, which is what makes §5.4 and §5.5 possible without a
world loaded.

#### 5.3.7 Text input, generalised

Exactly one text field exists — the catalogue search box — and it is spread across three
places: drawn at `InventoryScreen.cpp:452-491`, hit-tested by `insideSearchField`
(`.cpp:637-645`), and edited inline in `main()` at `Main.cpp:3162-3188` and `:3210-3215`
with a `kMaxQuery = 22` cap. Generalise it once:

```
struct TextField {
    std::string text;
    int caret = 0;
    bool focused = false;
    std::size_t maxLength = 32;
    bool (*accepts)(char) = nullptr;   // nullptr = any printable ASCII
};
bool handleTextInput(TextField&, std::string_view typed, KeyEvents);   // returns true if changed
```

- Source of characters is the existing `window.consumeTypedText()` (`Main.cpp:3172`); source
  of editing keys is the key path, which is exactly why `Backspace` and `Enter` are already
  in `engine::Key` (see the comment at `Window.hpp:55-56`) and why §5.3.0 must add the rest.
- Caret: a 1 × 9 art px white quad after the caret glyph, blinking 0.5 s on / 0.5 s off.
- Filters: `isSeedChar` (`[-0-9]` plus letters for text seeds), `isWorldNameChar` (printable
  ASCII except the Windows-illegal set `\ / : * ? " < > |`).
- **Migrate the search box onto it in the same slice.** Two text-editing implementations is
  bug shape #14 and this is the cheapest moment it will ever be to avoid.

#### 5.3.8 Scrolling, generalised

```
struct ScrollState { float offset = 0.0f; float contentHeight = 0.0f; float viewHeight = 0.0f; };
```

Reuse `Renderer::setClippedScreenMesh` (`Renderer.hpp:121`) exactly as the catalogue does,
and copy the catalogue's wheel/stick handling (`Main.cpp:3929-3956`) and its
`catalogueMaxScroll` clamp (`InventoryScreen.cpp:629`). The only additions are a draggable
scroller thumb and keyboard paging. Scroll snaps to whole rows on lists, is continuous on
the settings body.
